lead: Both readings look beneath the surface. Paul reminds the Corinthians that he came to them not with polished rhetoric but with the message of Christ crucified, so that their faith would rest on God’s power and not on human cleverness. In Matthew, Jesus teaches that what defiles a person is not food taken in through the mouth but evil that comes out of the heart. God looks at the heart; the Cross is the power that changes it.

r.h: Nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified
set: Corinth was a rich, busy port city where public speakers were admired for their eloquence. Paul founded the Church there around AD 50–51, after his visit to Athens (Acts 17–18). By the time of this letter the Corinthians were dividing into parties around favourite preachers (1:12). Paul has just said that the message of the Cross is foolishness to the world but the power of God (1:18), and now he recalls how he first preached to them.
str: vv. 1–2: not lofty words; only Christ crucified.
v. 3: Paul’s own weakness and fear.
vv. 4–5: the Spirit and power, so that faith may rest on God.
kw: A real textual variant in v. 1. Some ancient manuscripts read “mystery”, others “testimony”. The NRSV follows “mystery”; the POC follows “testimony”. Both fit Paul’s thought.
A perfect participle: Christ remains the Crucified One. The risen Lord still bears his wounds (John 20:27).
A technical word of the schools of rhetoric for a convincing proof. Paul’s proof was not an argument but the work of the Spirit in the lives of those who believed.
vv: I did not come proclaiming the mystery of God to you in lofty words or wisdom.
Paul was not against learning; he was against anything that puts the preacher in place of the message.
For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
This is not a narrowing but a centre. Everything Paul teaches, the Resurrection included, flows from this.
And I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling.
The great apostle was afraid. God’s strength showed itself in his weakness, as the Lord would tell him: “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.
Faith built on a speaker’s charm falls when the speaker fails. Faith built on God stands.
ch: The Church has always read these verses as a rule for every preacher and catechist: the aim is not to win admiration but to bring people to Christ. St Augustine, himself a trained teacher of rhetoric, taught in On Christian Teaching that eloquence must serve truth and that the preacher’s life speaks louder than his words (in substance). The Catechism teaches that faith rests on the authority of God who reveals, not on the evidence of human reasoning alone (CCC 156).

r.h: What comes out of the heart
set: Some Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem have asked why Jesus’ disciples do not wash their hands before eating, as “the tradition of the elders” required (15:1–2). This ritual washing was a matter of religious purity, not hygiene. The Pharisees were devout men who wanted to bring holiness into daily life. Jesus’ dispute with them is a debate within Judaism about what God truly asks. Today’s reading is his answer, first to the crowd, then to the disciples.
str: vv. 10–11: to the crowd: not what goes in, but what comes out, defiles.
vv. 12–14: the disciples report the Pharisees’ offense; the plant not planted by the Father; blind guides.
vv. 15–20: to the disciples: the heart is the source of evil; washing hands does not defile.
kw: Literally “make common”, that is, unfit for what is holy. Jesus moves the question of holiness from the surface to the heart.
In the Bible, not only feelings but the inner centre of the person, where thought, will and decision are found.
Peter calls the saying a parable (v. 15): a short, puzzling word that needs to be opened. The disciples still need to be taught.
vv: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but it is what comes out of the mouth that defiles.
Words come from the heart. A person is known by what comes out of him: speech, attitudes, actions.
they are blind guides of the blind.
A warning to every teacher in the Church first of all. Those who guide others must first let themselves be enlightened.
But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this is what defiles.
Jesus does not despise outward practice; he teaches what gives it value.
to eat with unwashed hands does not defile.
Mark, telling the same story, adds that by this Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Matthew, probably writing for a community close to Jewish practice, keeps the focus on hand-washing.
ch: The list of evils in v. 19 largely follows the order of the second part of the Ten Commandments: murder, adultery, theft, false witness. Jesus is not abolishing the law but bringing it to the heart. The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that the heart is the seat of the moral personality (CCC 2517), and it says that the New Law purifies the heart, the root of human acts (CCC 1968).

study: Does my faith rest more on a favourite preacher or on the power of God? What would change if that preacher were gone?
Jesus says evil comes out of the heart. What have I said or done this week that shows me what my heart needs?
